title: Right view
hookLine: knowing dukkha, its arising, its ending, and the way (MN 9)
last: EIGHT SPOKES — ALL MEET AT THE HUB.

cards: Put on someone else's glasses and the world tilts. The edges blur, the floor seems closer, you reach for a cup and miss. Nothing in the room changed.
Only the lens did. Right view, the first factor of the eightfold path, is about the lens.
And a long explanation of it comes not from the Buddha but from Sariputta again, in a talk where the monks keep asking, politely, for more. Each time, he finds another way to say it.

teach.h: DITTHI: VIEW, A WAY OF SEEING.
teach.b: The Pali is samma ditthi. Ditthi means view: a way of seeing. Samma, as we've heard, means right, complete, fitting.

The talk is the ninth in the Middle-Length Discourses. Sariputta asks: in what way is a disciple of right view, whose view is straight? The monks ask him to explain, and he does it in a pattern he repeats again and again.
When someone understands the unwholesome and its root, the wholesome and its root, that is right view.
Good, friend, say the monks, but might there be another way? Yes, he says, and explains it through food and nourishment.
Then through the four truths: understanding dukkha, its arising, its ending, and the way to its ending. Then through each of the twelve links: aging and death, its arising, its ending, the way.
Around and around, the same four-part shape. So right view here isn't mainly a set of opinions to sign. It's a way of looking at anything: what is this, where does it come from, can it end, and how?
Another sutta in the Connected Discourses, defining all eight factors, gives the short form: right view is knowledge of dukkha, its arising, its ending, and the way. That's the lens.
The four truths aren't only a teaching to remember.
They're also glasses to see through. A bad night's sleep, a fight with a sibling, a fear about money: each can be looked at the same four ways.
For Sariputta, that's what makes a view right: it looks at anything in terms of where it comes from and how it ends.

how: The Sammaditthi Sutta, Sariputta's talk on right view, is studied in Theravada monasteries, and teachers in several schools describe right view as seeing through the lens of the four truths.

o: seeing with the four truths as a lens

games.q: match the pieces of right view.
p: knowing dukkha, its arising, ending, way

s: in MN 9 Sariputta gives only one explanation of right view
the monks keep asking for another way, and he gives many, all with the same shape.
right view can be defined as knowing the four truths
that's the short form given in the sutta that defines the eight factors.
right view here mainly means signing up to a set of opinions
it's a way of seeing anything: what it is, its source, its ending, and the way.

games.q: you're one of the monks. Sariputta has just explained right view through wholesome and unwholesome roots. what do you ask?
o: but might there be another way to explain it?
which teacher is right about this?
games.why: the monks keep asking for another way, and Sariputta keeps finding one: food, the four truths, each of the twelve links.

practice: Bring to mind one small thing that happened recently and bothered you, and look at it four ways, a few breaths each: what is it, plainly; where did it come from; could it ease or end; what would help?
The answers needn't be perfect. Just try on the glasses, and notice whether the event looks different through them.

wordCard.voice: Samma ditthi. Right view: knowing dukkha, its arising, its ending and the way, the four truths used as a lens. The first factor of the path.

orig.note: Pali sammā diṭṭhi: right view, the first factor of the eightfold path.

carryVoice: Your line: see it as it is. Four questions make a lens for almost anything. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: MN 9 (Sammaditthi Sutta, Sariputta on right view)
